#1256. Mauricio Pochettino's USMNT farewell was inevitable but it hurts all the same: 'A big thank you from my heart'

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Two weeks after the U.S. men's national team failed to qualify for the 2018 World Cup, an in-depth look at the man who would become the team's head coach seven years later was available on bookshelves across the U.K. and, eventually, everywhere else. "Brave New World" by Guillem Balague is just as much a glimpse at the 2016-17 Tottenham Hotspur team as it is at a manager on the rise in Mauricio Pochettino, who cut to the chase in a handwritten note before the first chapter.

"Football is," he wrote, "or at least to me, a context of emotions."

There is supposed to be something ruthless about a sports team at the peak of its powers, and Pochettino's are no exception. He has built high-intensity, attack-minded teams for the better part of two decades, now on both sides of the Atlantic Ocean, but he has never tried to strip humanity out of a profession that unnecessarily demands an emotionless approach to the job. It is why, at U.S. Soccer's national training center in Atlanta on Friday, he began to cry.

"The human being is in front of everything," he said, "and that is why that is a really difficult decision, but we need to move forward. But a big thank you from my heart."

Pochettino finally booked his exit from the USMNT and will join Manchester United next week after two final games in the U.S., a two-legged Concacaf Nations League quarterfinal against Haiti on Saturday and Tuesday. Though United's approach only began on Sunday, after Pochettino and his staff arrived in Atlanta for the latest international break, the move was in some ways years in the making -- he had longed for a return to the Premier League, and as the USMNT's first coach with genuine international appeal, he had already turned down several offers before the Red Devils came calling. He was never destined for a long stay with the USMNT, even if the four-year deal he signed in August indicated otherwise, and U.S. Soccer knew as much by including a $10 million buyout clause in the latest contract.

Call it What You Want: A weekly podcast where Jimmy Conrad, Charlie Davies and Tony Meola cover all things USMNT and the state of the beautiful game in the United States. Catch the show YouTube live every Tuesday and Friday at 10 a.m. ET.

The predictability, though, did not lessen the pain.

Pochettino did not answer questions about his legacy or discuss the appeal of the United job, but two years after U.S. Soccer's surprise coup, he finally offered a hint at why the USMNT gig appealed to him outside of the paycheck and excitement of a World Cup on home soil. He became the USMNT's head coach a few short months after exiting Chelsea despite the turnaround he was overseeing one year into the role -- he and the club's owners did not see eye to eye on what was next, and as a result, he initiated his own exit. He was one of several high-profile coaches in Europe's club game to drop out of that realm of the sport. Jurgen Klopp left Liverpool on a high and told CBS Sports a year later that he did not miss a thing about coaching, but he recovered from the mental exhaustion just in time to take the Germany job in late summer. Carlo Ancelotti is now in charge of Brazil, Thomas Tuchel is currently the England coach and Pep Guardiola also left Manchester City after a storied decade. Burnout was something at least a few of them name-checked on the way out, and in his own way, Pochettino concurred on Friday.

"I think the most important thing is all that we left here [are] the moments that we share together," he said. "All the things that we accomplished. The things that we put in place. All the standards, all together, we increased in that federation and around the world, too, maybe. I didn't prepare [this] speech. I am talking with my heart and I want to say a big thank you ... because we recovered our motivation. We recovered our capacity to dream big, the capacity to train players that really want to improve and really want to share good moments and players that really care about the federation and this country."

If Klopp's timeline is anything to go by, two years appears to be the exact amount of time a coach needs to recover from the demands of soccer's most high-pressure environments before badly craving a return. Pochettino's U.S. arrival was a boon for the players, who had lost their way after a group-stage exit at the Copa America but now make up a team that has as clear a path forward as any. Forward Folarin Balogun said as much on Thursday, when Pochettino's exit was all but confirmed.

"I think things have been working well," he said. "We have a clear sense of identity, we have a clear playing style, and whenever you have a top coach, you'd want him to stay, as it's a no-brainer, so I think for us it's no different."

As it turns out, though, this job was just as meaningful for a coach who seemed to feel a little lost himself. In "Brave New World," Pochettino established that there is no distinction between the person and the coach. "Football has made me who I am and who we are as a family," he wrote. "It's what we wanted and what we chose to be. The ball has to be our travelling companion."

It is no wonder, then, that he needed a reset somewhere. Some will quibble that the USMNT job should not be the place for a mental reset, but the way Pochettino describes it, it was the right job at the right time for all involved. He did not describe the post as a break from his real calling but rather as one that reminded him why he got into this career in the first place. It is perhaps why United, a perilous job in which most are destined to fail, has its charms for a person like Pochettino. He feels ready for what might be an impossible job, and the window to take it before he becomes a has-been to Europe's top clubs is fleeting. There is also an undeniable truth about the profession Pochettino has chosen -- job security is a fictional concept and so failure is the only guarantee. Someone else's shortcomings are the only way to get a job in the first place, something Pochettino admitted as he celebrated a year with the USMNT in October 2025.

"I think we knew something [was] wrong here because if not, the federation, why [would] they call us?" he said at the time. "Why [would] they offer the job, no, really with not too much time to build our ideas, set our principles [for] the World Cup?"

U.S. Soccer has a fairly long runway this time to land a replacement, with the next World Cup just under four years away. The players, though, might feel left in the lurch for the time being as they watch a coach they really enjoyed working with say an abrupt goodbye. As Balogun put it on Thursday, "If I had a vote, I would like to keep things the way they are."

Pochettino's tenure was hardly perfect. The shockingly bad results outweighed the impressive ones, but most of the games landed somewhere in the unremarkable middle. There was plenty of hand-wringing along the way, from an almost incessant period of trial and error to his insistence that players be fully committed to the project when he would say things that led people to question his dedication. He also never got the team to a long-awaited World Cup quarterfinal, failing to reset the energy after the Balogun affair sucked the confidence out of the group. Yet he left quite the impression on some of the players he worked with. Take Sebastian Berhalter as an example -- he was as far away from the national team's radar as it gets when Pochettino first worked with him last year but has only hit stride after stride since. He credits Pochettino's belief in him for the rise, which is perhaps why he was nearly as emotional as the coach himself when he spoke on Thursday.

"Personally, on the field and off the field, he's done a lot for me, and from day one he's always believed in me. Before I set foot on the field, I think about the way I play and the way that I try to carry myself," Berhalter said. "He just said it doesn't matter what you're doing on the field; these are already the right things. And to be honest, I can't thank him enough, and regardless if he's coach, not the coach, and I say it every time that he's meant so much to me. And he's helped me develop as a player and as a person, and as a player, that's all you can ask for: to have that trust and have that belief in you. And for me, it's easy to go out there and just do my job, so he's meant a good deal to me for sure."

It only makes the question of where U.S. Soccer goes from here so pressing. This was not a perfect tenure, and yet it hit the sweet spot of what all parties needed at this moment in time. That clearly includes Pochettino, who enjoyed the best of what the U.S. had to offer along the way, a celebrity of sorts in his own right. Maybe long stretches in the Southern California sunshine during the World Cup had an oversized influence, and "Take Me Home, Country Roads" slaps too hard when 60,000-plus sing it together. Whatever it was, the vibes, at their very best, were special. It is hard for a self-proclaimed "emotional guy" to deny that, even if he feels life needs to take him elsewhere.

"When this type of moment [arrives], [these] always are tough, tough moments because [these] are not easy decisions. Normally, it's the opposite. You know you will be sacked and you cry because you want to stay," he said. "A big thank you from my heart ... because you always were transparent and always you always put in front the interests of the federation but always trying to build something together and we really enjoyed. We learned a lot from you, from you all, from this country, [these] amazing people. Yes, I think it was one of the most difficult decisions in our careers."

#1255. Brighton underline title credentials with impressive win over Man City

This Brighton and Hove Albion title challenge – as it must now be classed – flies in the face of the saying that money always talks in football. Manchester City have been found guilty of breaching financial rules and also fielded the most expensive midfield in Premier League history here, yet the match-winners cost a fraction in comparison.

Looking at Brighton’s winning goal, it was created by a cross that flashed across the City goal from Diego Gómez, an £11m signing who was playing in Major League Soccer in the United States not so long ago. Maxim de Cuyper, a £17.5m arrival from Club Brugge, was credited with the assist after Yasin Ayari tapped in.

Ayari cost £3.5m from Swedish club AIK and scored in the 5-0 wins over Coventry and Palace, and now has this winner to add to his collection. The 23-year-old is another example of Brighton polishing these gems and putting them together in a team that can win against any opponent in the Premier League.

It could keep them at the top end of the table for a good while longer. They have already shown they can defeat Arsenal in a one-off match and they look to have the ingredients to stay the pace with them. In Fabian Hürzeler they have one of the brightest young coaches in the Premier League and he has a squad that are all on the same page.

Leicester upset the odds 10 years ago with a settled team, while this Brighton team has a deeper squad. When the substitutes came on in the second half, they slotted into a well-rehearsed system.

“We faced adversity. There was a little bit of luck but in the end they deserved it because they worked hard for it,” said Hürzeler. “I want players who want to compete, to dominate. They all have the winning mentality inside of them. These kinds of performances are not about one or two players, everyone has to stick together.”

LOVE THIS TEAM SO MUCH! 🤩 https://t.co/QdBXsW1Ze5

Hürzeler has played down a title challenge but his team have been among the most impressive in the first part of the season. The German coach, 33, has been in English football for two years but has learnt quickly the tried-and-tested response of taking each game as it comes. Next is Getafe in the Europa Conference League on Thursday.

While Hürzeler was reluctant to name individual performers, Dutch goalkeeper Bart Verbruggen was another key player in this win. He kept out Iliman Ndiaye and repelled Erling Haaland, who lost a physical battle with Lewis Dunk. “You’re going down with the Palace,” chanted the jubilant Brighton fans, with City now losing two Premier League games in a row.

City head coach Enzo Maresca will be content with the number of chances his team created but there must be concerns at the other end. He tried a change of formula, dropping Marc Guéhi to the bench for the first time this season, yet his team were still prone to individual errors.

“We are the second team in scoring in the Premier League. We are scoring goals but in this moment we are conceding silly goals. We can avoid that,” Maresca said. His team have conceded 10 goals in their last six games, which is not the foundation of a title challenge, even if City have been stacking up points.

Maresca picked a midfield that cost £327m to recruit this summer, with Elliot Anderson, Enzo Fernández and Ayyoub Bouaddi picked together for the first time. There were some signs they could all play together, although City looked more dangerous when Rayan Cherki came off the bench to break up the trio.

Pascal Gross cost a nominal fee when he returned to Brighton but his hard work and intelligent passing means Brighton can control periods of the game even against the very best.

The goal came when Brighton switched play from a free-kick, although City thought Anderson was victim rather than perpetrator. Former Inter Miami winger Gómez provided the cross that opened up City, with Gianluigi Donnarumma guilty of not coming out to claim the ball, then Matheus Nunes slipped at the vital moment.

“Unfortunately it is happening for our players but I think it is part of the game, part of football, it happens many times against us, we need to analyse and understand what we can do better,” Maresca added. City also felt Dunk used his arm to block the ball in the penalty area, although no spot-kick was given.

It was a sweet goal by Ayari, who had missed a penalty in the shoot-out last week when the teams played in the EFL Cup. Brighton stayed in Manchester after the defeat, masterminding a win that means they have now defeated all of the traditional heavyweight teams in the Premier League.

“I wasn’t aware of that. For me it’s more important, not about history, it’s about giving something back to the supporters. They’ve spent a lot of time and money,” Hürzeler said.

“We’ll take it game by game. See what happens because we have loads of games. Just focussing every day on what’s ahead of us and the job we have. We will continue to do that and see where it leaves us at the end of the season. We are happy with the way we are playing - not just the results but the way we are playing too. We have to continue to develop that style and ruthlessness and we can do great things.”

#1254. Inside football's Christian revolution: The Premier League stars who say God has saved them from their darkest moments, stopped them diving to win penalties - and why some still face mockery and abuse for their faith

Published: 20:04 EST, 13 November 2026 | Updated: 05:14 EST, 14 November 2026

When Borussia Dortmund star Felix Nmecha transferred an imaginary crown from his head onto the pitch last weekend, he probably wasn't expecting to spark a firestorm.

Arriving at the German national team camp two days later, he was summoned for a grilling by sporting director Rudi Voller and manager Jurgen Klopp. His symbol of surrender before God, a goal celebration called ‘The King’s Return’, had blown up into an international news story.

Voller, alongside many of Dortmund’s fans, was concerned by Nmecha's ties to Ballers in God, a network of Christian players founded in 2015 by former Tottenham midfielder John Bostock.

While its core mission is to promote faith in Jesus, the evangelical group is believed to hold a conservative stance on issues such as sexuality and gender – a perspective Nmecha has been in hot water for promoting before.

Nmecha insisted that his message was one of love, but as his celebration was dissected worldwide, the furore posed more questions than it answered. What role does the Christian faith play for footballers? What impact is the groundswell of belief having on dressing rooms? And what should teams do when ancient creeds clash with modern culture?

For months, Daily Mail Sport has been speaking with Christian players, chaplains, and academics. We have found that some footballers are still mocked in dressing rooms for their beliefs. We have also heard tales of elite stars praying with non-League journeymen, and of faith sustaining players through injury crises and rescuing them from dark places after their retirement.

Borussia Dortmund midfielder Felix Nmecha attracted controversy in Germany for his 'The King's Return' celebration against Elversberg last Saturday

Manchester City winger Jeremy Doku is one of a growing number of practising Christians in the Premier League

For many players, their beliefs and careers are inextricable. Brentford forward Igor Thiago thinks it was part of God's plan for his father to die so that he would become a footballer and share his beliefs internationally.

'If my father were alive, I do not think I would have become a footballer, because I think he wanted me to be someone else,' Thiago tells Daily Mail Sport. 'It wasn’t until later that I understood there was a purpose for me to come here and be someone else. To be Thiago, who is a footballer, who can speak about God for so many people, in another language.'

Thiago worked as a fruit-carrier, bricklayer, and rubbish collector from the age of 13 in the streets of Gama, Brazil, to provide for his family after his dad passed away. A career in the Premier League was unimaginable back then. Now he is the main man at Brentford and one of several players at the club professing a Christian faith.

And they are not alone in their devotion. Across the top six divisions, 75 per cent of clubs have a Christian in the first team and almost half regularly host Bible studies or prayer meetings, according to a survey of 134 outfits by Christians in Sport.

Their director, Graham Daniels, remembers being told in the 1980s that he was one of just four openly practising Christians in the professional game. An impossible claim to verify, but yes, you read that right, just four. Now you have starting XIs containing more believers than that – and we hear some managers have even been attending church with their squad members. 'There’s a real movement of God within football,' one chaplain at a professional club tells us.

Perhaps God is dwelling in the treatment room, too. Bournemouth winger Ben Gannon-Doak has had three major injuries in his career – to his knee, then quad, then hamstring – and credits his growing faith for helping him recover from each blow.

'With the first, that was before I was strong in my faith – I didn't cope with that one well. I was 17 and felt lost without being on the pitch,' the 21-year-old tells Daily Mail Sport.

'The quad injury, I coped better because I started slowly practising my faith more. When my hamstring injury came, I was closer to God than I had ever been before and I coped with that very easily, it was much easier mentally than the other two. I was able to play in the World Cup after that.

Brentford forward Igor Thiago thinks it was part of God's plan for his father to die so that he would become a footballer and share his beliefs internationally

Arsenal's 'Bible Brothers' are the most famous band of Christian players – around 10 of their stars including 'pastor' Jurrien Timber (left) pray together before matches

'I believe all my injuries happened for a reason and I coped with them the way I did for a reason. I just need to trust God. It makes you stronger, prepares you for things, tests your character. It changes you. Faith has impacted my life in the best way possible.’

Multiple footballers interviewed for this piece cited the Bible verse Philippians 4:13 – 'I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me' – as a key driver in their life. Gannon-Doak has it tattooed on his left arm.

Football has always had crossover with religion – Manchester City and Everton are among the many clubs to have started as church teams, for example – but the past few years have seen it assume more public prominence.

Arsenal's 'Bible Brothers' are the most famous band of Christian players – around 10 of their stars including 'pastor' Jurrien Timber and Noni Madueke pray together in the hotel before matches, and regularly share Bible verses on social media. Organisations such as F3 and Ballers in God, who hold daily prayers and weekly Bible studies, have built Christian fellowship across the divisions.

'Premier League players are on the same call with guys who are semi-pro at step four,' Omar Beckles, a player for League Two Gillingham, tells Daily Mail Sport. 'Lads got together virtually during the pandemic and have been consistently since.' But why the explosion of Christian expression now?

‘An important factor has been the increasing number of players coming from Africa or Latin America, where Pentecostalism and other forms of evangelical Christianity are strong,’ Hugh McLeod, Emeritus Professor of Church History at the University of Birmingham, explains to us.

‘Chaplains interviewed for an academic study in 2011 claimed that elite footballers had “a disproportionate passion for the faith” compared with the average member of society, and they saw the players who had come in from other continents as having a big influence on this.’

An earlier generation of Christian players graduating into management positions, as well as a broader shift in Gen Z asking the cosmic questions in life, has opened up football to the tender matters of faith. Group Bible studies, or even stoppages for Muslim players to break their Ramadan fasts, were unheard of until recent years.

'Christians in a changing room can be frowned upon,' says Steven Sessegnon, the Fulham academy graduate who now plays for AFC Wimbledon. He was mocked for being baptised

Marc Guehi was reprimanded by the FA after writing 'Jesus loves you' on Rainbow Laces armbands enforced by the Premier League in support of the LGBTQ+ community

Daniels, who is now a director at Cambridge United, says Christian values have earned players respect in the dressing room – and thinks faith could alleviate the turmoil players face when the final whistle blows on their career.

‘There was tremendous bullying in the 1980s and 1990s, but the more people saw authentic Christianity, the more they realised that it didn’t harm the changing room, but made it better,' he tells Daily Mail Sport. 'Their integrity shone through – players felt if they talked to Christians, they wouldn’t gossip, and they’d be caring, and they wouldn’t be judgmental.

‘In football your identity is achieved. You're as good as your last game. It’s too much pressure for players. That’s why people gamble, drink, and divorce when they retire, because you spent your life having to prove yourself and you don’t know what to do with yourself when you can’t anymore.

'Or think about the academy players who are released at 16. You were the best kid in your class, then your town, your city, your region, the academy system. Then they are released and disappear from the game. Their identity is shot. They feel shame and failure for the rest of their lives.

'If you know your identity and your purpose is a received gift from God, it’s a complete contrast to everything you’ve ever imbibed. He's going to use your highs and lows in sport to draw you closer to Himself. He’s given you this vocation – this is your gift from Him and He loves you.'

Beckles concurs. ‘Being a Christian actually gives you an unfair advantage in football because you’re always living with some form of optimism and hope,’ he tells Daily Mail Sport.

‘You know there’s no despair. Setbacks are an opportunity to improve and go again. When my dad died, I really saw God show up. He granted me a level of peace and grace and joy just to function at that time when I was grieving.’

That said, there is clearly an occasional tension between faith and football, which can bring fame, wealth, and temptations untold. Pele, for example, was very open about his low-maintenance relationship with Christianity's bedroom bylaws.

Meanwhile, Daily Mail Sport has heard of stars who have felt compelled to switch church after becoming Premier League regulars as they had become too recognised and overwhelmed by their original congregation.

City star Antoine Semenyo has a close relationship with pastor John Thompson and was baptised on a beach in Bournemouth last December

Then there's the minefield of political and social issues which footballers are scrutinised over. When playing for Crystal Palace in 2024, Marc Guehi was reprimanded by the FA after writing 'I love Jesus' and 'Jesus loves you' on his Rainbow Laces captain's armband, the wearing of which was enforced by the Premier League in support of the LGBTQ+ community.

And that brings us back to Nmecha. He could have simply pointed to the sky, or made a sign of the cross, when celebrating against Elversberg last Saturday. It wasn’t his expression of faith, but rather the specific King’s Return action associated with Ballers in God, which riled a certain crowd. No matter that other players, such as Nottingham Forest's Jair Cunha, have deployed the celebration without incident. Klopp says that after their talks, Nmecha will not be repeating it. Dortmund executives will be breathing a sigh of relief.

The website for The King’s Return campaign initially linked to a live counselling chat run by conservative evangelical organisation Groundwire. There, counsellors espoused the beliefs that homosexuality is sinful and abortion is ‘Satan’s plan’. When Daily Mail Sport investigated the chat service, we were met with similar views.

It is not fully clear if Ballers in God agree with Groundwire, or if their members even assume a uniform theological position on such issues, but the network celebrated the scrapping of the Rainbow Laces initiative by the Premier League last year. They appear to have removed the link to the Groundwire chat in the wake of the Nmecha controversy. Daily Mail Sport made repeated requests for an interview with founder Bostock, who has been described as ‘hard to pin down’ and a ‘busy man’, but was turned down.

While high-profile incidents are a PR headache for clubs, there is no need for contrasting moral codes to disrupt a team’s cohesion. ‘You might not agree with someone, but you can respect them and treat them in a non-discriminatory way,’ says Dr Keith Parry, Principal Academic in Sport at Bournemouth University.

‘We’ve had openly gay players and referees at the top level in rugby. It is strange that men’s football is different, but questions around sexuality and inclusion go deeper than religion.

‘There are so many barriers (to players potentially coming out) such as toxic masculinity, fans making homophobic remarks, and so on. There are a lot of Middle Eastern and conservative North American owners in football – how might that impact on inclusion? It depends on the owner.’

Beckles, who has represented 14 clubs, believes Christian players have a duty to let love rather than division shine through. ‘Footballers are constantly in a world where there’s someone not far from them who will want something from them. Their manager and fans want them to perform, people want their signature, people want them to give them money, their agent wants commercial growth,' he tells us.

Bournemouth and Scotland star Ben Gannon-Doak (right) has the verse 'I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me' tattooed on his left arm

The young winger credits his faith with helping him through three major injuries

'It’s nice to meet someone that doesn’t want anything from them and genuinely cares for them eternally. That level of love should set people apart.'

Despite dressing rooms becoming more tolerant of faith, some players still face derision. 'Christians in a changing room can be frowned upon or mocked,' says Steven Sessegnon, a player for League One side AFC Wimbledon, who was taunted after being baptised while at a previous club.

'You hear some real nasty things. Some boys don’t understand, which we give them grace for. What scares me the most is why people get so worked up about footballers who are believers.

‘We’re not bothering anyone. We’re going about our business in a loving and caring way. It really rubs people the wrong way and it can cause arguments inside the changing room. One boy was told he will never play because he’s too soft, because he’s a Christian.'

On matchday, faith is increasingly visible and impacts how players go about their business. The temples are not always glamorous – we hear that some players have even met in the sanctuary of a broom cupboard to squeeze in prayer. Clubs offer what they can. At League One Plymouth, they take the analysis suite – at Arsenal, they have a multi-faith prayer room. Across the pyramid, prayers often ask for protection from injury and the chance to glorify God – but not for a win.

At Championship Charlton, six to eight players read the scriptures and pray together. 'They have God-given talents and want to use them as an act of worship,' says club chaplain Matt Baker, who is also on hand at the training ground on Fridays to pray with players. 'When you see players do the sign of the cross after scoring a goal, they see it as evangelistic, but it's also expressing to God that I'm doing this for you, for your glory.'

At Exeter City in League Two, chaplain George Baker tries to spread the love around the club. 'I'll do the rounds of the stadium and chat to the stewards and grounds staff,' he says. 'It's a great opportunity to value the people who are making matchday happen.’

Beckles says that religious considerations even factor on the field. 'How do you live with a level of integrity when you want to win? It’s winning in the right way. The “dark arts” are really difficult to navigate,’ he tells Daily Mail Sport, and he is not the only player to express this feeling to us.

'Being a Christian actually gives you an unfair advantage in football because you’re always living with some form of optimism and hope,' says Omar Beckles (right)

‘In my heart of hearts, I’d like to think I wouldn’t dive to win a penalty – that’s deception. I try my best not to do any of that. But there is the heat of the moment that exposes our nature.’

Gannon-Doak adds: ‘Players losing their temper, starting fights, that's the stuff I try to avoid. But some of the dark arts, that’s just part of the game.’

A popular Christian slogan since the 1890s goes as follows: ‘What would Jesus do?’ Typically it is applied to quandaries in a believer’s life – how to treat somebody who has seriously wronged you, for instance.

Not as often has it been wondered: ‘Would Jesus go down if a sweaty centre-back tugged his shirt in the penalty box in the 90th minute?’ But the next time you catch a game, you might just catch an athlete wrestling with that kind of question. What would you do?

#1253. Mauricio Pochettino leads USMNT in two-game farewell against Haiti after taking Manchester United job

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

While the winds of Manchester United swirl around the United States men's national team, there's still soccer to be played as a place in the Concacaf Nations League semifinals is on the line. Mauricio Pochettino will be managing his final games in charge of the national team, finishing out his tenure with the two matches against Haiti before returning to the Premier League. Given that Steve Cherundolo is currently with the U-23 side in Spain, there's no viable interim head coach that the USMNT could have gotten in before Tuesday anyway, meaning that Pochettino gets an unconventional farewell tour before leaving for Old Trafford.

The message from players such as Chris Richards and Antonee Robinson is that they're professionals, and considering that Richards could be going back to a new manager at Crystal Palace following the break, these are elements of the game that they're used to dealing with. That professionalism is important when the singular focus has to be on getting past Haiti and into the Nations League semifinals.

I already expected Pochettino to lean on the World Cup core of the roster in the first match, but given the vibes around the USMNT, it's even more important that they get off to a good start, as any doubt that's left opens the door for the noise from outside camp to set in. They've already dealt with this, considering the AC Milan rumors that cropped up ahead of the World Cup, and that will only make the squad more prepared to go out and perform even with the issues at hand now.

If Pochettino determines that they can't start the match, there could be shifts in the XI, but the only player I see starting who wasn't a World Cup regular is Sebastian Berhalter.

With Gio Reyna withdrawn from the squad due to injury, Berhalter can deliver set pieces while also producing from the center of the pitch. He was one of the best performers from the September and October international breaks and has gone back to Middlesbrough and kept up his form, which should be rewarded during this camp. Sergino Dest has also left camp due to an injury, which leaves the wings a little lighter than expected, but Malik Tillman's versatility will come in handy as the Bayer Leverkusen man can fill any midfield position.

#1252. Mauricio Pochettino leaves incomplete legacy as USMNT tenure nears finish

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

He raised the standard of U.S. Soccer. It's the first thing that you hear from multiple people as Mauricio Pochettino prepares to oversee his final two games. The reality is more mixed. His 1.91 points per game are the third-best of any manager to oversee the United States men's national team for more than 10 games, behind Gregg Berhalter and Bruce Arena, but he's also the first permanent manager since Steve Sampson to not win a Concacaf title, with the USMNT falling short in both the Concacaf Nations League and the Concacaf Gold Cup. That said, it's hard to say that he isn't leaving the USMNT in a better place than he found it, although some credit should be given to U.S. Soccer and former sporting director Matt Crocker for that. It's a conflicted legacy that Pochettino will leave, but it's also one that can't be fully realized until after he oversees his final two matches against Haiti.

If his departure overshadows the performance on the pitch, leaving the USMNT without a chance to win the Concacaf Nations League final for a second consecutive tournament, that will undo a significant portion of the good that he has accomplished by bringing along younger members of the squad. But as he prepares to depart, the USMNT exited the World Cup in the round of 16, the same stage as in 2022, and questions remain about how they'll hold up against the world's top teams. With the 2028 Olympics coming up and a new training facility that allows space for the youth and senior sides to train in the same place, alongside the improvement in U.S. youth development thanks to MLS Next and MLS Next Pro, the USMNT were going to be in a good place no matter who took over at this stage, which is also what makes it critical to look at what comes next.

Date: Saturday, Nov. 14 | Time: 4:30 p.m. ET Location: Nu Stadium -- Miami, Florida TV: TNT | Live stream: HBO Max Odds: Haiti +750; Draw +440; USMNT -350

"Our ambition is high, and we believe that this is one of the great coaching jobs in the world. We have an experienced group of players; we've got a dynamic young pool of players," U.S. Soccer CEO JT Batson said. "Last night, Mauricio, staff, and most of the men's team watched our U-20s play here at the national training center, which was a pretty special moment. We publicly shared our ambition is to be in a position where we're winning major tournaments, including World Cups, and we want to make sure that we're attracting leaders who help us do just that. We know from our experience that great leaders want to work with great people, and great leaders want to make an impact on things that matter, and we think that we've proven at U.S. Soccer that we're a great place to work and we're a great place to make legacy-defining impact."

Call it What You Want: A weekly podcast where Jimmy Conrad, Charlie Davies and Tony Meola cover all things USMNT and the state of the beautiful game in the United States. Catch the show YouTube live every Tuesday and Friday at 10 a.m. ET.

U.S. Soccer is still in talks to hire a director of soccer who will work with the incoming head coach, United States women's national team coach Emma Hayes and the rest of the U.S. Soccer staff to shape the vision of American soccer. The sport is growing rapidly here, which is what makes this such an attractive job even without the shine of hosting a men's World Cup on home soil to add to the sales pitch. Listening to Batson, while BJ Callaghan may be one of the top American fits for the role, you can easily see why the USMNT would like to bring in Pep Guardiola if they can, and there's a sales pitch there to at least get top targets to pick up the phone.

This doesn't diminish what Pochettino has done while leading the national team, but each manager has made his mark on American soccer in his own way. Jurgen Klinsmann added legitimacy to the USMNT role and ushered in an era of German Americans who led the squad to new heights. Gregg Berhalter came in, raised the floor for the squad, did excellent work with dual-national recruitment and led the squad out of its group at the 2022 World Cup in Qatar. Sure, in hindsight, things should've ended there, with U.S. Soccer moving in a different direction after the World Cup, but the players also wanted continuity.

You can make the same argument that Pochettino maybe shouldn't have been signed to a new contract following the World Cup, but even he seemed to believe that an opportunity such as Manchester United wouldn't have come this quickly. If he were leaving in 2028, after Steve Cherundolo led the U.S. U-23s on a strong run in the Olympics, the departure wouldn't be as bittersweet as this one, which feels like a job left unfinished by the Argentine.

Pochettino did add confidence, and to hear players like Sebastian Berhalter, Cavan Sullivan, Alex Freeman and Neil Pierre, among others, tell it, when Pochettino was at his best, this team would press anyone off the pitch. Now the onus is on the players to take that forward under new management.

"I think Poch definitely raised the standard since he's been in charge. I think you guys have seen that, just the intensity of training, how we approach games, he's changed our way of thinking as players, from calling the friendlies that we have in certain camps official games, not official games. He wants us to just be of a mindset to go out there and win," Folarin Balogun said.

"He's laid the foundation, and I think we, as players, have that ownership to not just do that because Poch was in charge; I think we have the ownership as players to carry that out because we know the standard," he continued. "So yeah, I think that's the benefit of having a top coach, and I'm sure you know whether he's here or not, the US will look to replace him with another top coach."

A tearful Pochettino and the disappointed players show that this didn't end the way anyone would've wanted, but that doesn't mean there isn't plenty of good to build on for whoever comes next. With Cherundolo leading the December camp, there's plenty of time to ensure that the next hire is the right one, but now that U.S. Soccer has shown that it can recruit a coach of Pochettino's caliber, there's no reason to stop there. Having a coach coveted by others is a product of success, but having a system that can move past that proves things are sustainable.

The word "sustainable" hasn't been one that U.S. Soccer has been able to use as of late, as one thing going wrong could lead to a spiral, but with benefactors, facilities and youth all at once, it's time to build a future that isn't dependent on who the coach is, because that's what will lead to winning a World Cup.

#1251. Why is 46-year-old Ronaldinho returning to soccer with Ravenna, an Italian third division club?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Ronaldinho, one of the greatest footballers of all time, will be back on the pitch on Sunday, Nov. 15, for a historic day. The Brazilian striker, who won the 2005 edition of the Ballon d'Or and played for PSG, Barcelona and AC Milan at the peak of his European career, signed a deal in the summer of 2026 to join the roster of Ravenna, an Italian team currently playing in the third division. Ronaldinho, who played his last professional match in 2015 and will turn 47 next year, is expected to play some minutes in the home derby against Forli, and you can watch it all on Paramount+. But let's break down how and why he's coming back to play after more than a decade and after announcing his retirement in 2018.

"I'm really looking forward to this moment and coming back to Italy once more."@10Ronaldinho says he can't wait to return to professional football with Ravenna at age 46 💪 pic.twitter.com/0UMdkhgFlY

Ravenna, who have a history of playing in Italy's lower divisions, were acquired in 2024 by Ignazio Cipriani, the nephew of Arrigo Cipriani, the founder of the iconic Harry's Bar in Venice. The Cipriani Group operates high-end restaurants, private members' clubs (Casa Cipriani), luxury hotels, event venues and branded residences across major international cities, such as New York City, London, Monaco, Miami and Dubai. Basically, it is now positioning itself as a global luxury lifestyle and real estate player, rather than simply a restaurant group.

"Today I do a lot of Footy Volley. I'm training differently."The legendary @10Ronaldinho talks coming out of retirement after 11 years to suit up for Ravenna in Serie C this weekend 👀 pic.twitter.com/z0cSOHd2k4

This is why Cipriani created links with some of the most notable figures in the world: soccer players, politicians, singers, actors and more. When the group entered the world of soccer, it brought in people who had already worked at the highest level of the game, such as former AC Milan sporting director Ariedo Braida, who played a key role alongside former AC Milan CEO Adriano Galliani in building AC Milan's legacy under Silvio Berlusconi's presidency. Braida left AC Milan in 2013 after 27 years.

Ravenna's current head coach is Andrea Mandorlini, who spent several years coaching in Serie A and represented Inter as a player between 1984 and 1991. The connection with Ronaldinho, who joined AC Milan in 2008 during Braida's tenure at the club, also involves another key figure at Ravenna: Lorenzo Tonetti, the club's head of external relations. During Ronaldinho's time at AC Milan, Tonetti owned Giannino, a restaurant in Milan that became something of a second home for several of the club's players. It was also a favorite meeting place for Galliani, who famously negotiated several transfer deals within its walls. Curiously, one of the waiters working there at the time was Giuseppe Riso, now one of the best-known agents in soccer, who represents players such as Sandro Tonali, Davide Frattesi and Carlos Augusto.

Ronaldinho signed a dual player-investor contract in the summer of 2026. He joined Ravenna with the ultimate aim of scoring one final professional goal while also acquiring an ownership stake in the club. Rather than having him play every week, his deal focuses on global marketing and special appearances in marquee matches, such as the local derby against Forli that will take place on Sunday. Ronaldinho is one of the most notable players in the history of the game. He joined Barcelona in 2003, where he became a global superstar, winning two FIFA World Player of the Year awards, the 2005 Ballon d'Or and the UEFA Champions League in 2006. In 2008, he moved to AC Milan, where he played until 2011. At the international level, he was a key part of Brazil's national team that won the 2002 World Cup. He formally retired in 2018 but played his last-ever football game three years earlier, in 2015.

#1250. Washington Spirit clinch third consecutive trip to NWSL Championship with win over Utah Royals

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

After two runner-up finishes at the NWSL Championship, the Washington Spirit will get a third consecutive shot at lifting the big prize.

The Washington Spirit rallied from an early deficit to defeat the Utah Royals 2-1 in front of another sold-out Audi Field. The Spirit weathered the fastest goal in NWSL playoff history, then flipped the script within minutes and never took their foot off the pedal or lost control. Utah Royals' Cloe Lacasse struck first on the scoreboard, and Sofia Cantore and Clara Luvanga provided the decisive goals for the Spirit, while Trinity Rodman brought plenty of spark and Andi Sullivan supplied reliable, steady play in the midfield.

Here's how the Spirit rallied for the win:

The Royals arrived in D.C. early in the week, avoiding a nationwide flight stoppage on Friday, and fresh off a huge quarterfinal upset -- a 1-0 win against the No. 2 seed San Diego Wave FC. They wasted little time to show their early playoff win was no fluke.

In the opening two minutes, Utah won a corner kick, and Lacasse created multiple moments of history. Her service into the box curled toward the near post, creating some miscommunication between goalkeeper Sandy MacIver and her defenders, and the ball snuck into the net. It was the fastest goal scored in NWSL playoff history and the first-ever olimpico scored in the postseason.

CLOÉ LACASSE OLIMPICO IN THE SECOND MINUTE 😱@UtahRoyalsFC off to a FLYING start the @NWSL semifinal!Watch the action LIVE on @CBS and @paramountplus! pic.twitter.com/UfWxDcSB5Y

The early breakthrough stunned the typically rowdy crowd, though the set-piece tally was hardly a surprise, considering Utah's ability this year. The squad scored 15 goals off set pieces this season, with seven headed goals, so Lacasse's ability to score from the flag was just one more highlight for its set-piece playbook.

The early lead should have been a boost for the visiting side, but instead, it opened up the game; the Spirit then tested the Royals with relentless attacking pressure.

The Spirit needed just six minutes to turn things around. Washington's attacking trio combined for the equalizer, with Luvanga finding Rodman out wide in space, and the winger quickly connecting with Cantore in front of goal.

SOFIA CANTORE WITH THE BACKHEEL 🤯Her seventh goal of 2026 is her first playoff goal to bring @WashSpirit level 1-1!Watch the action LIVE on @CBS and @paramountplus! pic.twitter.com/C8J63tVzQn

"I think getting scored on in the first few minutes will really humble you, and a little bit of a wake-up call, but I thought our response was incredible right after and all game long," Sullivan said after the game.

"As soon as we responded after the goal, I think even when we got scored on, I had full confidence that we would get it done," she said.

Sullivan's role in controlling the game as the Spirit closed out the first half was notable. She's the longest-tenured player on the active Spirit roster right now, with goalkeeper Aubrey Kingsbury out on maternity leave. Sullivan herself returned to the squad after an ACL injury and then maternity leave. The defensive midfielder completed all of her tackles (three) and aerial challenges (four) and captained the team on the pitch.

"She represents a lot of the values that we want to have as a team, as a club, on and off the field, and right now she's reaching that peak of performance. I'm very, very happy and proud of her because it's been tough for her. Obviously, coming from a long injury, and then maternity leave. So being able to come back to get fit again and try to compete at this level; it's not easy, and she's a role model. An example as a captain with the young players, new players, and being able to do a lot of things," Spirit head coach Adrian Gonzalez said after the game.

"Whatever the team needs, she's kind of that voice. Very happy and proud of her because I know what this means to her and also for us. Having her again and being able to play a final is huge for her and for us," he said.

While Utah managed to stave off attacking sequences by the Spirit to close out the opening half, the Spirit's game-winning goal came in the early minutes of the second half. A poor back pass by Utah in their own half was the final dagger. Luvanga pounced on the mistimed pass, and a smart touch inside the box beat goalkeeper Mandy McGlynn.

CLARA LUVANGA POUNCED ON THIS PASS 😮‍💨Her second goal in her second playoff match and the @WashSpirit are one step closer to returning to the @NWSL Final!Watch the semifinal LIVE on @CBS and @paramountplus! pic.twitter.com/f0uUfUU19K

The Tanzanian international has only been on the roster since September, but her impact on games has grown week to week, and now she can add a game-winning NWSL playoff goal to her resume.

"It's not the first one that she scores like that. Obviously, she puts a lot of pressure on centerbacks, keepers, and that is very contagious. When you see that your forward is pushing and jumping and pressing like that. Everyone who is behind they follow her, and also creates a lot of doubts and nerves on the opponent team, not facilitating the build-up. And obviously, that was, I think, a big shot of energy," Gonzalez said after the game.

"I think it was also a little bit of release, knowing that 'okay, we did the most difficult thing' that was coming back after we conceded a goal, and yeah, happy again because she's bringing a lot. Both attacking and defending, and obviously she's learning so quick and having a huge impact."

What's next The Spirit will face the winner of Sunday's semifinal between Gotham FC and the Kansas City Current. This will be the Spirit's third consecutive appearance in the NWSL Championship. When the league announced a neutral site for the 2026 NWSL Championship, it selected Audi Field, and now the Spirit have a chance to play in a home playoff final on Nov. 21.

#1249. Inside the new life of 'conflicted' Arsene Wenger after he turned down the fight against Gianni Infantino: His 'divorce' from Arsenal and why he could still walk away from FIFA's gravy train

Published: 12:00 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 12:00 EST, 16 November 2026

Next week Arsene Wenger will be in Qatar for the second staging of FIFA's 48-team Under-17 World Cup.

He described last year's inaugural event using one evocative word. 'Paradise,' he said. 'Basically, 25 per cent of the football world was here.'

At the end of last month – as the fall-out from FIFA president Gianni Infantino's foiled plan to sell off parts of the men's senior World Cup rumbled on – Wenger was in Azerbaijan at the hosting of the very first Under-15 version.

An eight-a-side tournament with the emphasis on technique and quality, it was – in his role as FIFA's head of global development – another of his own ideas. According to those who know him, this is Wenger's happy place.

'Arsene's vision is very simple,' one long-time ally tells Daily Mail Sport. 'It has always been that as many boys and girls as possible can participate in the game under as good a quality of coaching as is physically and financially possible.

'That is it, basically. That is why he works for FIFA. He wants that direct influence on the game. He is 77 but fundamentally he is a coach at heart. In his own mind, he still has his whistle in his mouth and his stopwatch round his wrist.'

Arsene Wenger is FIFA's head of global development and many thought he'd challenge Gianni Infantino for the presidency of the organisation. Those hopes were misplaced

Wenger, the former Arsenal manager, is still a coach at heart according to those that know him well

Viewed in this context, it is perhaps not a surprise that Wenger is no longer expected to stand as a rival to Infantino at next March's presidential elections in Rabat. The deadline for nominations is on Wednesday.

Wenger's fury at what he saw as Infantino's World Cup treachery was limitless. Some close to him feared he may quit in protest at an organisation he joined seven years ago. Others urged him to challenge Infantino's presidency, hoping it would serve to cleanse FIFA's reputation for sleaze.

But even though as recently as last week Wenger's intentions remained unclear to many people within the organisation, the conflict raging inside his own head was crystal clear.

'Arsene is an idealist and a romantic,' explains another source who has known him for 20 years. 'And the head of that organisation is not a place for someone like that. FIFA presidency is about glad-handing and politics and – let's face it – money.

'Say what you like about Infantino, he's good at it. It's his natural habitat. He knows the rules. Arsene? He would lie awake at night wondering where all the money was going. He would be fretting about whether it was being spent in all the areas the different confederations told him it was.

'On the one hand, Arsene would be a perfect figurehead for the global game. A purist. The total antithesis to Infantino's perceived chicanery. But in reality, how much could he change? Many of FIFA's reputational issues are deeply embedded.'

The sub-plot to Wenger's emotional conflict regarding a direct challenge to Infantino is that inside FIFA it has had an all or nothing feel to it. The former Arsenal manager's contract in his current global development role expires at the end of this year and for all that the organisation would very much like him to renew, there remains the possibility that he may walk away.

If Wenger doesn't – as we now expect – stand in opposition to Infantino, will he have the appetite to continue working underneath him?

Wenger was furious with Infantino's foiled plan to sell off parts of the men's senior World Cup

Wenger with the Premier League trophy in 2004. 'Arsene would be a perfect figurehead for the global game. A purist,' says a source who knows him well

Wenger, for example, was a noticeable absentee when other FIFA leaders gathered to support Infantino at a management committee meeting in Morocco in August. The two men were not seen together again until they stood side by side at the Under-15 tournament last month.

'I think that (Wenger's future) is a very pertinent question,' adds another ally. 'It's on his mind and it's a big decision. To a much lesser degree, his age may well be a factor too. But he has the fire in his belly. He has energy. I know that.

'He had a certain aim and certain targets when he started with FIFA. And he hasn't met them yet.'

Under Wenger's stewardship and guidance, FIFA have established 60 academies in previously under-resourced football backwaters such as India, Uzbekistan and New Caledonia.

'We provide the structure, the finance and – by way of top coaches – the expertise,' explains a source from the governing body. 'For example, we have Spanish coaches leading the way in India. We basically have coaches coaching the coaches, if that makes sense.

'Arsene believes every child in the world should have a pathway if they have the talent. India, for example, have never been to a senior men's World Cup. Arsene wants to change that.'

At last month's Under-15 World Cup, 500 players were involved who had emerged from Wenger's FIFA academies. The governing body's stated aim is to have established 75 by the end of next year.

'In Arsene's mind, the number would actually be 100,' laughs his associate. 'And he knows he isn't there yet.'

Spain, watched by Infantino (left), raise the Under-15 World Cup in Azerbaijan last month

The Under-15 World Cup was one of Wenger's ideas and is an eight-a-side tournament with the emphasis on technique and quality

Wenger is evangelical about it all. Some would – and do – say he remains a dreamer at heart. He also remains a small details person. For example, the reason he has established the Under-17 World Cup as an annual event is that he doesn't want a single talented footballer to fall through the cracks and miss out simply by being born a year too early or too late.

The Frenchman is not, however, without his contradictions. Once asked privately how a father of a daughter could justify a FIFA decision to hold the 2034 World Cup in Saudi Arabia – where the women's rights issue remains deeply contentious – Wenger suggested that he wished only to 'effect change from within'.

Just as pertinent is the impact Wenger has undoubtedly had – for better or for worse – on football's global calendar. You don't have to have a particularly sharp memory to recall the many times Wenger railed against the dangers of too much travel and playing-time on his top players when he was in charge at Arsenal.

Of all the top English clubs, Arsenal were the last to commit to arduous pre-season tours to places like America and the Far East and that was simply because Wenger was the manager. He always preferred a week in the Austrian mountains to a schlep round the world.

Now – eight-and-a-half years on from his departure from the Emirates – Wenger has been firmly attached to FIFA's gravy train for some time, a driving force behind the expanded summer Club World Cup and a key advocate of a plan to hold the World Cup every two years that ultimately didn't get off the ground.

Wenger is on record on the matter. 'The welfare of the players in the last 20 years has increased dramatically,' Wenger has said. 'When you look at injury prevention, recovery work, nutrition and advances in medical technology. It is unrecognisable from what it used to be.

'Also VAR has helped with the protection of players, as players know they cannot escape from making bad tackles that cause injury.'

Club coaches across Europe may raise eyebrows at that. So would many of those who opposed the expansion of this year's World Cup to 48 teams. But alternative theories are also in play.

Asked how a father of a daughter could justify the decision to hold the 2034 World Cup in Saudi Arabia – where women's rights are deeply contentious – Wenger said he only wished to 'effect change from within'

Many wanted Wenger to challenge Infantino's presidency, hoping it would serve to cleanse FIFA's reputation for sleaze

'Arsene was seen as poster boy for the two-year World Cup and, yes, he put his weight behind it,' explains our FIFA source. 'But in truth we were being asked that question by some member associations. It was FIFA's duty to look into it.

'The mistake some people make is to look at everything from a European perspective. European football is blessed but not everybody is. Many countries just don't play as much competitive football and Arsene is strong on the global view.

'He listened to the pushback but wants to give opportunities to clubs from smaller nations in things like the Club World Cup and a bigger World Cup. It's not just about England, France, Germany, Argentina and Brazil.

'When you are a club manager you are paid to be essentially selfish and when he looks back he recognises that. His horizons have been broadened. Some of the smaller nations don't have the calendar congestion that exists in England, for example.  His principles remain the same but he has just seen another perspective.'

By his own self-effacing admission, Wenger has always led a rather monastic existence. Splitting his time between Zurich – where FIFA have their HQ – and his home in the north London enclave of Totteridge, he still endeavours to run 5km every morning. After that, it's football.

'If there is football on TV from one of the leagues then I will watch it,' he told Mo Farah on a recent episode of the Olympic Champion's podcast. 'It's simply what I like to do.'

It is not too simplistic to say that the sport remains Wenger's obsession. It is hard to imagine him without it at the core of his life. Equally, it is difficult to imagine a return to club football in any meaningful capacity.

The wounds caused by what he felt was a rancorous departure from Arsenal have healed but that, nevertheless, remains a chapter closed.

'Arsene was seen as poster boy for the two-year World Cup and, yes, he put his weight behind it,' explains our FIFA source

'Sir Alex Ferguson was capable of staying tight to Manchester United but for Arsene and Arsenal it was different'

'It would be disingenuous to say it wasn't all a bit distant and uncomfortable for a while,' says a source with knowledge of the situation. 'Arsene made a decision to step away from it completely. Sir Alex Ferguson was capable of staying tight to Manchester United but for Arsene and Arsenal it was different.

'The ending was different for a start. So it was a bit like a divorce. You need some distance for a while before you can remember what you liked about each other back in the first place.

'But that's where it is now. It's thawed. There is semi-regular contact. He's been back to a game, even if it was just the one.'

For Wenger, the pull of what he sees as unfinished business with FIFA may remain strong. Equally, beyond the rather waspish and phlegmatic public face has always run a river of steel.

'You don't go toe to toe with Fergie all of those years and have all that personal c**p poured on you by Jose Mourinho and come out the other side in one piece if you haven't got some proper b***s,' says one of our sources.

'Some of us were surprised how long it took him to come out and speak publicly about his opposition to Infantino's World Cup sell-off. It was discussed. But he got there in the end. The bottom line is that he has his principles and he already has his relevance. Infantino constantly has to fight for his. Arsene does not. If he isn't comfortable where he works, he will always find something else.'

It's a view thoroughly endorsed by just about everybody in Wenger's orbit. 'Whatever he does next – whether with FIFA or somewhere else – it will be in football,' adds an ally. 'The next chapter will be his decision. He is very focused. And there is already a legacy.'

'The bottom line is that Wenger has his principles and he already has his relevance. Infantino constantly has to fight for his'

Wenger and Infantino will in all likelihood be side by side in Doha next week as the second staging of FIFA's 48-team Under-17 World Cup gets into full swing

Wenger and Infantino will in all likelihood be side by side in Doha next week as the Under-17 jamboree gets into full swing. Teams from Tanzania, Mozambique and Vietnam will make their debut in the 104-match tournament. In Qatar, FIFA will present a thoroughly united front with Wenger's avowed principles at its core.

'You can play with an orange or you can make a ball with paper,' Wenger told The Independent in a rare interview three years ago. 'That's why football is so popular. But today if you want to get to a good level of education in football, in some countries you don't get it.

'I find that not right because, in many countries, there are some private initiatives, but the parents have to pay to get the children in there and play. For me, it doesn't matter if you're rich or poor. If you are good, you come in.

'Our academies are free, just open to talent. You have to adapt and find a solution in every country.'

#1248. Spurs win three in row for first time in 616 days to pile pressure on Sage

For the first time in 616 days, Tottenham Hotspur have won three Premier League matches in a row. Three different managers have been sacked in that time, and the mood in north London had plunged to grim lows, but finally there is a sense that something truly exciting is stirring at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium.

This victory over Crystal Palace was not as impressive as last week’s triumph at Chelsea, but it did not need to be. After Palace striker Jean-Philippe Mateta was sent off in the 13th minute, Spurs simply had to make their numerical advantage count. They did so with relative ease, taking complete control of possession and creating endless goalscoring opportunities.

Roberto De Zerbi’s team ended the night with 34 shots to Palace’s two and with 758 completed passes to Palace’s 149. The goals ultimately came from two defenders, Archie Gray and Jan Paul van Hecke, but there was a long list of Spurs players who might have scored here.

Spurs take the lead through an Archie Gray header! ⚪ https://t.co/qSCECkOJur

Did this defeat mark the end for Pierre Sage, the Palace manager? The Frenchman was only appointed in June but it has been a grisly start to the campaign. Palace have the worst defence in the league, have lost six of nine games and have not produced any truly encouraging performances in the Premier League.

Even in the two games Palace have won, against Fulham and Nottingham Forest, they were lucky to do so. The likes of Sean Dyche and Thomas Frank, both of whom would be strong candidates to replace Sage if Palace do pull the trigger, will no doubt have been keeping an eye on events here.

“I am really aware of the situation,” Sage said. “I don’t like this situation. [But] you can trust in me, I will never give up. I want to be the first on the pitch on Monday. I have the rage to train more. It’s not me to decide this thing [his future]. If I have one hour, I will give my best for one hour. If I have 10 years, I will give my best for 10 years.”

The decision for Palace chairman Steve Parish, then, is whether this result represented a continuation of the team’s problems or was an aberration caused by the early red card. It would be reasonable for Sage to claim this match was out of his hands from the moment Mateta lunged at Spurs captain Micky van de Ven, but such an argument might not carry much weight with Palace sitting 18th in the table.

The challenge was foolish in the extreme by Mateta, a player who was much more successful in exiting this game than he has been in his numerous attempts to leave Palace in recent transfer windows. At first glance it did not seem the worst tackle, but the replays were damning: Mateta led with his studs and made forceful contact with Van de Ven’s ankle.

It was an inexcusably brainless act, after just 13 minutes of play, and the same could be said of Palace’s defending from a right-wing corner a few minutes later. Mohammed Kudus swirled the delivery to the back post, where Gray was unmarked. Yes, Palace were defending with 10. But no, that does not justify the inability of Sage’s players to spot Gray. Even more embarrassingly, the Tottenham player was unmarked again from another corner shortly afterwards.

It was not the first time this season that Palace’s cause has been undermined by a red card. When they lost at home to Ipswich Town in September, Axel Disasi was sent off after 34 minutes. An absence of discipline? Perhaps. Sage might argue, though, that he is not responsible for his players demonstrating a lack of basic brainpower.

Jean-Philippe Mateta receives his first red card for Crystal Palace! 🟥 https://t.co/U9UYb29mbk

All of this was welcomed heartily by the Spurs fans, who celebrated Mateta’s dismissal as though it was a goal. Recent results have restored some of the enthusiasm in this corner of north London and the mood here was buoyant, even before Gray’s opener.

“Now we are playing as a team,” De Zerbi said. “Before the international break, we were playing as many good players but not as a team. We showed our maturity. We are improving.”

The second goal was always coming and it arrived in the 73rd minute, when Van Hecke attacked a wonderful cross by Mateus Fernandes. Palace goalkeeper Dean Henderson saved the first attempt but the ball dropped onto the head of Van Hecke, now seated in the six-yard box, and he happily nodded it home.

Jan Paul van Hecke doubles Spurs' lead! 👊 https://t.co/1Odkkr8wBJ

The new signings at Spurs endured a difficult first few weeks but there were more signs here that they are adjusting to De Zerbi’s system. Sandro Tonali was exceptional in midfield and teenage talent Luca Williams-Barnett also sparkled off the bench. “Tonali was unbelievable,” De Zerbi said. “We played with two players more: Tonali was double.”

Spurs face Leeds United, Ipswich Town, Sunderland and Fulham in their next four league games. The momentum could, and perhaps should, continue to build. Their optimism here contrasted sharply with the angst of Palace, and with the troubled look that was etched on Sage’s face.

“Very pleased for the performance, very tough game. You don’t know 11 [against 11] would be different game but Crystal Palace are very tough because they defend with a low block, no space and we showed we are a mature team. Maybe we could score more goals with more nastiness, but I am very happy because we created many chances. We need more goals for sure. It’s not enough, but we are improving a lot.

“I was very nervous before the game, during the game, after the red card, it’s always better playing with one player more. But today, against this team, they played with this behaviour, all behind the line of the ball, aggressive. Very tough game.”

When asked if Spurs are looking up the table, he replied: “We don’t forget the ambitions. We have to look behind what was the situation two weeks ago. In the last two years, two times 17th in the table, many games without a win in front of our fans. We have to stay focused. They are improving, increasing the level of performance.”

Speaking to Sky Sports, the Palace defender said: “Definitely was frustrating. It was one of the first tackles of the game. And we felt like we were doing well and it is unfortunate. We go again.

“The main message was don’t concede again, stay tight as a defence and try to hit them on the counter. That is the best plan when you’re down a man.

“Unfortunately, it didn’t happen today. We know what we can do as a team, as a back five, the whole unit. There were some positives in the games, but I can’t say much when you lose. We just have to go again.

“Hopefully, the next game we win. The main message is to stay together as a team. We know what we are capable of. It is staying confident and bouncing back.”

"We want to be back at the top again" Jan Paul van Hecke reacts after Spurs win three consecutive Premier League games ⚪ https://t.co/XXOeOKLhoC

Tottenham have won three Premier League games in a row for the first time in 616 days 📆 https://t.co/krb7tkrPyM

Tottenham are up to eighth, while Palace are in the relegation zone on goal difference.

Pedro Porro continues to venture forward and smacks a half-volley over from a tight angle. Spurs make the game’s next change as former Palace loanee Gallagher replaces Solanke, with Marmoush moving up into the striker position.

Roberto De Zerbi, the Spurs head coach, had some good news for the supporters on Friday when he said that James Maddison was fit and available despite being taken off at Stamford Bridge. “This week he didn’t work like the other players, but for tomorrow he is available and he is a special player for us. A special player because of the character and he has unique characteristics.

“For James Maddison or the players who are coming from a long injury, they have to work more than the other players, but he has already four or five weeks he is working very hard and consistently.”

While Tottenham are chasing a third successive league victory for the first time in 616 day, De Zerbi insisted there will be no complacency. “For me nothing has changed. We started this pre-season with a long project and we have to stay calm and clear in the head to work to build something better than when we came here,” he said. “One win or one defeat more, nothing will change. We have to analyse to improve the results but to improve the results we have to improve all aspects.”

Pierre Sage, the Palace manager, lightened the load after knocking Fulham out of the Carabao Cup in midweek but seemed surprised that the fans have remained so supportive. “It’s always a good sign,” he said. “I appreciate it [singing his name at Craven Cottage] very much and I can thank them but I prefer they are with the team than me alone. Because I’m the manager, but I’m not the most important part of the team, of the performance and the result. I think the players need it more than me but it’s really appreciated from me.”

Asked what he has learnt about fan sentiment from looking at social media, he said: “I think they understood what happened, why we are not perfect at the moment. We don’t care who is the most responsible for the situation. I take the responsibility. I have no problem with that. I just want people to understand what we do and why.”

Two changes from the starting line-up that took on Newcastle: captain Dean Henderson is back in goal and Oscar Mingueza replaces Anan Khalaili at right wing-back.

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of this Premier League encounter between Tottenham and Crystal Palace.

Last weekend, Spurs enjoyed a historic result, beating Chelsea 2-0 at Stamford Bridge for only the second time in the league for 36 years thanks to Mike Penders’ own goal and Mathys Tel’s stunning solo strike. This result, coupled with the 3-1 victory over Coventry City in their previous home outing, means that Tottenham have won back-to-back league games and are beginning to gather some momentum under Roberto De Zerbi.

In his pre-match press conference, when asked if he’s felt a change in atmosphere after the triumph at Stamford Bridge, De Zerbi replied: “We have not achieved our goal. We want our fans to be happy, not now, at the end of the season. Now we have to push, we have to stay focused, we have to increase the spirit, the appetite to win games in a row. To do that, we have to show if we are good enough. If we are good enough on the pitch, for sure we are ready. In the head, in the mentality, we have to show, because the step of this club is to win games in a row and to be angry day by day, game by game, win by win. One time or two times are not enough.”

Palace have endured a tricky and inconsistent start to the season under their summer appointment Pierre Sage, accumulating just seven points from their opening seven league matches while shipping 17 goals. The 1-0 League Cup victory over Fulham in midweek has momentarily eased the pressure on the Frenchman, but given their newfound success in recent campaigns, fan expectations have risen, with recent performances prompting some cause for concern.

Tottenham remain without the suspended Rodrigo Bentancur, while Xavi Simons, Wilson Odobert, Lucas Bergvall, Savio, Tosin Adarabioyo and Mykhaylo Mudryk are out injured. James Maddison was substituted early in the second half at Chelsea with an apparent groin strain, but De Zerbi insists he’s available for this one. Destiny Udogie could also be involved after recovering from a knee issue.

The visitors are without the injured trio of Ismaila Sarr, Takehiro Tomiyasu and Chadi Riad, but there’s hope that Quinten Timber and Jorgen Strand Larsen are fit to be involved this evening after they both missed the Fulham victory.

Kick-off is at 17:30, with teams coming shortly.
